units.title: Division with remainders
units.description: See division through dot arrays and k-tables, and master the remainder rule.
learningObjectives: Write the division relation with dividend, divisor, quotient and remainder
Build a k-table to list multiples of a divisor

blocks.text: When 17 dots are shared into rows of 5, three full rows appear — and 2 dots are left over. The leftover dots are the **remainder**.

blocks.label: 17 dots in rows of 5
blocks.description: ●●●●● ●●●●● ●●●●● ●● — three complete rows of 5 and one partial row of 2, so 17 = 3 × 5 + 2.

blocks.text: The remainder is always smaller than the divisor. If the remainder equalled or exceeded the divisor, another full group could still be removed.
A **k-table** lists multiples of the divisor as k × divisor for k = 0, 1, 2, 3, … It turns division into a search: find the largest k whose multiple still fits inside the dividend.

content.text: The largest multiple of 5 that fits in 42 is 40 (k = 8). Two dots remain, so 42 ÷ 5 gives quotient 8 and remainder 2.

blocks.question: What are the quotient and remainder for 37 ÷ 6?
blocks.explanation: 6 × 6 = 36 fits inside 37, leaving 1. A remainder of 7 would be impossible — it is larger than the divisor 6.

units.title: Numbers with the same remainder
units.description: Describe every number that leaves remainder r when divided by d.
learningObjectives: Generate all numbers with a given remainder using d × k + r
Recognise same-remainder families in tables and number lines

blocks.text: Every number that leaves remainder 2 when divided by 5 sits exactly 5 steps from the next one. The complete family is described by one formula:

blocks.caption: Numbers leaving remainder 2 when divided by 5

blocks.text: Numbers leaving remainder r when divided by d are exactly the numbers d × k + r. Consecutive members of the family differ by d.

blocks.title: Worked example: is 128 in the remainder-3 family of 7?

content.text: 125 is not a multiple of 7, so no whole k works. Indeed 128 = 7 × 18 + 2 leaves remainder 2, not 3.

blocks.title: Subtract first, then divide
blocks.text: To check a remainder: subtract the remainder from the number, then divide by the divisor. If the subtraction gives an exact multiple, the number is in the family.

blocks.question: Which number below leaves remainder 4 when divided by 9?
blocks.explanation: 67 = 9 × 7 + 4, so it is in the family 9k + 4. The others give remainders 2 (65), 7 (70) and 2 (74).

units.title: Remainder puzzles
units.description: Translate verbal clues into remainder conditions and hunt down mystery numbers.
learningObjectives: Convert spoken clues into remainder families
Intersect families to find mystery numbers

blocks.text: Each clue in a puzzle selects a family of numbers. A mystery number must belong to **every** clue's family, so list the families and look for common members.

content.text: *I am less than 30. I leave remainder 1 when divided by 2, and remainder 1 when divided by 3. Who am I?*
Remainder 1 when divided by 2 means odd: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, … Remainder 1 when divided by 3 means numbers of the form 3k + 1: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22, 25, 28.
All five candidates are under 30. The step between common members is 6, and indeed 1 + 6 = 7, 7 + 6 = 13 — each leaves remainder 1 for both divisors.

blocks.text: Remainder puzzles become list-and-intersect problems: write each clue as a family, then find members shared by all families.

*I am between 20 and 40. Divided by 2 I leave remainder 0; divided by 3 I leave remainder 2.* Multiples of 2: 20, 22, 24, … Numbers of the form 3k + 2: 20, 23, 26, 29, 32, 35, 38. The common members are 20, 26, 32, 38 — four possible answers, and extra clues would pin one down.

blocks.question: A number leaves remainder 2 when divided by 5 and remainder 1 when divided by 4. What is the smallest number above 10 that satisfies both?
blocks.explanation: The 5-family with remainder 2 is 12, 17, 22, 27, … Testing in the 4-family (remainder 1): 12 = 4×3+0 ✗, 17 = 4×4+1 ✓. So 17 is the smallest above 10.
